name: cloud-morpheus
description: c3-morpheus on a phone: the cloud's workflow orchestrator. Four panels — the Dagu workflow list, the probe registry that declares what 'healthy' means, the fleet control panel, and the PM board (Paca). c3-watchdog keeps what is running alive; c3-morpheus decides what runs.
_doc: WHY MOSTLY WEBVIEWS, AND WHY THAT IS NOT A COP-OUT. Dagu and Paca are live authenticated surfaces that already draw themselves; Paca in particular has NO board API (/api/health, /api/v1/boards and /api/boards all 404, and every route 302s to auth.diegonmarcos.com behind Authelia forward_auth), so the board IS the Paca app and the SuperApp already renders it inline for exactly this reason. Reimplementing either would be inventing a second truth. ac_c3-watchdog is a WebView on the same reasoning.
_doc_no_dead_buttons: Every panel either shows a real surface or states on screen what is not wired and why. A page that fails to load renders an explanation, never a blank rectangle — which matters most on Boards, because Paca is mesh-only and a phone off the WireGuard mesh would otherwise show white space that reads as an outage.

surfaces._doc: The surfaces this app opens, as DATA. app/build.gradle turns each into a BuildConfig field; nothing here is a Kotlin constant, because a URL hardcoded in a class is a URL that gets copied and then diverges from the one the rest of the fleet uses. Mirrors the rule libs/ops follows for DAGU_DEFAULT_SERVER.
surfaces._doc_paca: MESH-ONLY. There is no public edge certificate for this name — it measures 000 from the public edge while the service is healthy on 10.0.0.6:8095. The app says so when the load fails instead of implying an outage.
surfaces._doc_superapp: The fleet control panel is the SuperApp's Constellation page, managing ~57 fleet apps. Morpheus hands off to it with a launch intent and says so when it is not installed. It deliberately ships NO second fleet updater: two updaters keyed on the same package ids would fight each other.

reuses._doc: What this app CONSUMES rather than reimplements. Each of these would silently diverge if copied, and the copy is always the one that goes stale.
reuses.dagu: The Dagu web UI, with Dagu's own Start button. The same server Cloud/C3/Observability reads through DaguClient.listDags().
reuses.probes: app/src/main/assets/probes.json is a committed MIRROR of cloud-u-linux/da_morpheus/data/probes.json, which is the source of truth. Mirrored, not fetched, because the APK must render the registry with no network; the file's own _mirror_of key says which copy wins.
reuses.paca: Rendered inline. There is no board API to wrap.

not_wired._doc: Stated here as well as on screen, so nobody has to launch the app to find out. NOTHING in this APK can start a workflow or a probe.
not_wired.triggering: Being built once in ab_cloud-libs-shared/libs/ops — Dagu POST /api/v1/dags/{name}/start with a fresh client_credentials token per run, plus a server-side GHA dispatch proxy. Morpheus will call that client rather than grow a second one to keep in sync with Authelia. Until then the Workflows tab shows Dagu's own Start button, which does work.
not_wired.live_probe_results: The Health tab shows DECLARATIONS. Live results come from the cloud-health-*.sh family, scheduled by Dagu and published to ntfy. A green tile drawn here would be a colour with nothing behind it.

android._doc_application_id: NEW app, so there is no update chain to break — but the fleet updater identifies apps by package id, so this is fixed from the first publish. The obvious mirror of com.diegonmarcos.watchdog.

modules._doc: settings.gradle iterates this (FIRE rule 6: never hardcode the list). One module. v1 depends on no shared library — pulling ab_cloud-libs-shared in now would add its whole build to this app's critical path for nothing. That changes when `run` gets wired and takes the trigger client from libs/ops.

toolchain._doc: Pinned for reproducibility, all derived in flake.nix. Mirrors ac_c3-watchdog / aa_cloud-superapp so every Android project here shares one toolchain story.

signing._doc: ONE shared Cloud-constellation signing key for ALL Android apps. The SAME key signs every app so cross-app signature-IPC and the in-app fleet updater never hit a signature mismatch. The raw keystore and its sops-encrypted passwords live ONLY in the private vault repo. build.sh::_resolve_signing reads $VAULT_DIR and sops-decrypts (SOPS_AGE_KEY), exporting ANDROID_KEYSTORE_* for gradle. THERE IS NO FALLBACK: without the key the build fails loud rather than shipping an app signed by a random key.

release._doc: Per-APK distribution, the same data-driven block every app here has. build.sh oras-push and gh-release read it; the workflow hardcodes no registry or tag. This block is ALSO what makes the app discoverable: aa_cloud-superapp/data/regen.sh admits a sibling on .android.application_id + .release.ghcr, so registering in the constellation is a property of the app rather than a list to edit by hand. {sha} -> git short sha, {version_name} -> android.version_name.

ghcr._doc: Login with GITHUB_TOKEN, never a PAT: a PAT creates an ACCOUNT-owned package that is born private and cannot be patched afterwards, because visibility is decided at CREATION and inherited silently forever. GITHUB_TOKEN creates the package FOR THE REPOSITORY and it takes the repository's visibility. This is a NEW package, so it gets exactly one chance to be created correctly.

auto_update._doc: The in-app updater reads release_url first and falls back to GHCR. NOTE: version_code in this file is 1 and never bumped by hand — the real code is computed in app/build.gradle from wall clock, which is what actually lands.

gh_release._doc: rolling_tag is canonical: one release the ship workflow overwrites on every main push, so /releases/latest/download/C3-Morpheus.apk is a stable URL.

variants._doc: Per-ABI variants with DISTINCT asset names. Without them both matrix legs upload one asset name to the rolling release and race: the second leg's --clobber deletes the first's asset mid-upload, and worse than the error, the winner is arbitrary — an x86_64 APK can land under the arm64 name and be installed on a phone.
